To report what others said with verbs like affermare, dichiarare, sostenere, precisare + che.
To choose the mood after the verb: confermare che + indicative, negare / smentire che + congiuntivo.
To use the present press conditional for unconfirmed information: sarebbe, avrebbe.
To use the past press conditional for an unconfirmed past fact: avrebbe acquistato.
To recognise source formulas: secondo, stando a, a quanto pare, pare che, si dice che.
To express the future in the past in reported speech: ha detto che sarebbe venuto.
Florence, late March. Pietro and Davide visit the newsroom of the "Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno", invited by Sandro Mancini. News from the agencies appears on a screen.
Here, boys, this is where the agency news comes in. Read this one.
"According to sources at City Hall, the mayor is reportedly against the new car park." Why "reportedly"? Is he against it or not?
We don't know for sure yet. The conditional is our way of saying: others are saying it, we aren't.
And when does it become certain?
When the news is confirmed by two different sources. Or when the mayor himself declares that he is against it.
And what if the mayor says it isn't true?
Then we write: "The mayor denied being against it." To deny means to say officially that something is false.
You need lots of different words to say "he said".
Exactly. To state, to maintain, to admit, to specify… Each one says something more. "He admitted" means he didn't want to say it.
Wait… look at this. "Via Maggio: according to unofficial sources, an entire building has reportedly been sold."
Let me see… "In the building, which houses a historic trattoria, flats for short-term rentals are reportedly planned."
But… that's the number of Grandma's trattoria!
S followed by M is voiced, like "zm": zmen-TEE-re.
"SC" followed by R doesn't soften: in-di-scre-ZIO-ne.
Stress on "VO": por-ta-VO-ce, with "ce" as in "chess".
In the press "ha detto" is too plain. Each verb adds a nuance:
Il sindaco ha dichiarato che il progetto è utile.
Gli abitanti sostengono che il quartiere sta cambiando.
La società ha confermato la vendita.
Il portavoce ha smentito la notizia.
Ha ammesso che ci saranno dei lavori.
Ha precisato che nessuno sarà sfrattato.
When you read an article, the reporting verb tells you what the journalist thinks. "Sostiene" sounds less certain than "ha confermato".
2. Indicative or congiuntivo after the verb
Ha confermato che il palazzo è stato venduto.
Ha negato che la trattoria debba chiudere.
Il sindaco ha smentito di essere contrario.
The logic is the same as in chapter 55: what is presented as certain takes the indicative, what is denied or doubted takes the congiuntivo.
Journalists use the conditional for information they have not yet verified. Just like the Romanian press: "primarul ar fi demisionat" (the mayor has reportedly resigned).
The mayor is reportedly in Rome.
La società avrebbe intenzione di vendere.
The company reportedly intends to sell.
The building has reportedly been sold.
La società avrebbe acquistato il palazzo.
The company has reportedly bought the building.
It is not a conditional of wishes or hypotheses: there is no "if". It only means "this is being said, but we don't guarantee it".
Secondo il Comune, i lavori durerebbero un anno.
a quanto pare / a quanto si dice
A quanto pare, il palazzo è stato venduto.
Pare che vogliano fare un albergo.
Si dice che il prezzo sia altissimo.
Fonti vicine alla società parlano di un hotel.
"Secondo me" (my opinion) and "secondo il giornale" (the source) use the same word. Context makes the difference.
When you report in the past what someone said about the future, Italian uses the PAST conditional (Romanian keeps the future):
Ha detto che il palazzo sarebbe stato ristrutturato.
Ha promesso che ci avrebbe fatto sapere.
Ha scritto che sarebbe arrivato il giorno dopo.
A typical mistake of Romanian speakers: "Ha detto che verrebbe" (present conditional). Correct: "Ha detto che sarebbe venuto."

The Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno newsroom was on the third floor of an old building near Santo Spirito, above a pharmacy. Pietro had imagined it like in American films: dozens of journalists running, phones ringing, someone shouting "Stop the presses!". Instead there were six desks, a half-dead plant, a coffee machine that sounded like a tractor and a ginger cat sleeping on a pile of old newspapers. "His name is Headline," said Mancini. "He's the only one here who never makes mistakes."

Davide had prepared his questions on a sheet of paper, in order of importance. The first was the one closest to his heart: whether drawings got paid for at the newspaper. Mancini laughed. "They do get paid," he confirmed, "but not much. Very little. But they are seen by thirty thousand people." Davide thought for a moment, then wrote on the sheet, next to the question: "Little, but thirty thousand." He decided that, all things considered, it suited him.

Then Mancini showed them how an article is born. First a piece of news arrives, from an agency, from a phone call, sometimes from a rumour heard at the bar. "Rule number one," he explained, "is that news must be checked. Two different sources, always. Until we have two sources, we use the conditional." He opened an article he was writing on the screen: "The new car park in Piazza della Calza has reportedly been rejected by the heritage authority." "Reportedly," he repeated. "Because only one person told me. Tomorrow, if someone else confirms it, I'll remove the conditional."

Pietro found it fascinating. "So the conditional is like saying 'it's not my fault if it isn't true'?" Mancini raised his eyebrows. "Put like that it sounds bad. Let's say it's an honest way of telling the reader: we've heard this, we haven't seen it yet." The editor, an elderly gentleman in red braces called Carlo Ferri, walked past at that moment and added: "And when a journalist forgets the conditional, along come letters from eleven-year-olds." Pietro went as red as the braces.

Davide, meanwhile, had drawn the editor: the braces, the glasses on the tip of his nose, Headline the cat on his head like a hat. Ferri looked at the drawing for a long time without smiling. Then he said: "This is a cartoon. A real cartoon. Young man, on Sunday we need a drawing for the culture page. Are you up to it?" Davide said yes so quickly that he dropped his sheet of questions. The cat, offended, moved to another pile of newspapers.

It was just then, while everyone was laughing, that a new agency report appeared on the screen. Mancini read it aloud, out of habit: "Florence, Oltrarno. According to unofficial sources, the property company Arno Living has reportedly bought an entire building in Via Maggio. In the building, which houses a historic trattoria, twelve luxury flats for short-term rentals are reportedly planned." Then he read the street number. Pietro stopped laughing.

"It's Grandma's trattoria," he said. "It's our home. Matei, Giulia and Viola live upstairs." Mancini looked at him, then at the screen, and his face changed. He picked up the phone and made three calls, one after another, speaking quietly. Pietro and Davide waited in silence. Even the cat seemed to be listening. After twenty minutes Mancini put the phone down. "The sale has been confirmed by two sources," he said softly. "It's not a conditional any more. I'm sorry, Pietro."

The two boys ran across Piazza Santo Spirito, turned into Via Maggio and burst into the trattoria out of breath. Graziella was making the sauce for the evening. Pietro didn't even say hello. "Grandma, the building has been sold! The agency said so! It's been confirmed by two sources!" Graziella kept stirring the sauce for a few seconds. Then she turned off the heat, wiped her hands on her apron and sat down. "I know, sweetheart," she said. "I've known for a month."

The story, told that evening in front of the whole family, was simple and sad. The building had belonged for more than a century to the Lenzi family, who had rented the premises to Graziella's parents in 1952. Old Mrs Lenzi, who came to eat at the trattoria every Friday, had died in December. The heirs, two grandchildren who lived in Milan and had never been to Via Maggio, had sold everything within a few weeks. In February a letter had arrived: the trattoria's lease, which expired in September, "would not be renewed on the same terms".

"And why didn't you tell us anything?" asked Marco, more hurt than angry. Graziella shrugged. "Because Pietro had his essay, Giulia and Matei had the workshop, the baby was teething. I thought I'd sort everything out on my own before you noticed." Matei looked up at the ceiling, towards Viola's little room, towards the notches on the door. Their flat was part of the building too. Nobody said it out loud, but they all thought it at the same moment.

The next day Mancini's article came out on page five, written with a caution Bellini called "textbook". The sale was presented as certain, without the conditional. But everything else was in the conditional: the twelve flats "would" be for tourists, the work "could" begin in autumn, the trattoria's rent "would" be tripled. At the end of the article was the company's statement. The Arno Living spokesperson had stated that "no final decision has yet been taken" and had denied that the trattoria "must necessarily close".

Bellini read the statement aloud in the trattoria over a coffee. Then he took off his glasses. "A lesson in journalistic Italian," he said to Pietro. "When a company declares that 'no final decision has been taken', it means the decision has been taken but not yet signed. And when it denies that the trattoria must 'necessarily' close, the important word is 'necessarily'. It means: it could stay, if you pay three times as much."

Meanwhile, in the neighbourhood, rumours were travelling faster than the agencies. At the newsstand they said a hotel would open in place of the trattoria. At the baker's they maintained it would be a sushi bar. Signor Franco had heard, from a cousin of a cousin, that the whole building would become a fashion museum. Davide's mother swore the new owners were American; the fruit seller, that they were Chinese; the barman, that they were "those people from Milan, which is worse".

Pietro listened to all these rumours with the new ear the newsroom visit had given him. "In the neighbourhood," he told Matei that evening, "everyone talks in the conditional, but without using the conditional. They say 'it's a hotel' when they should say 'it would reportedly be a hotel'. Mr Mancini would say they don't have two sources." Matei smiled for the first time in two days. "Mr Mancini would say they don't even have one."

Graziella, on the other hand, made no comment. She cooked. But when the fruit seller came into the trattoria and asked if it was true that a sushi bar would open in its place, Graziella put down her ladle and answered with a frightening calm: "A sushi bar instead of ribollita? Over my dead body. And I assure you, my dear, my dead body is very heavy." The fruit seller repeated the line all over the Santo Spirito market, and by the next day it was as famous as the ribollita.

Once again it was Mancini who came up with a proposal. He phoned one evening at dinner and asked to speak to Graziella. "Signora, it isn't only your trattoria in the neighbourhood. In the last two years the haberdasher's, the shoemaker's and the bookshop in Via Toscanella have closed. All for the same reason. If you agree, the paper will organise a public meeting. The residents speak, the company is invited, and the city council listens. At least, we hope it listens."

Graziella stayed silent for a long time, the phone in her hand. The whole family was watching her. Even Lupino, under the table, had pricked up his ears. Then she said only: "All right. But the meeting is held here, in the trattoria. And the ribollita is on me." When she hung up, Bellini, who had stayed for dinner as he now did almost every evening, raised his glass. "To the conditional," he said. "Because as long as something is in the conditional, it can still be changed."

The following Sunday, on the Gazzetta's culture page, Davide's first cartoon appeared. It showed a big steaming pot of ribollita with a sign on top: "Not for sale". Next to the pot, tiny, a man in a suit and tie was trying to lift it, without success. Underneath, the signature: "Davide, aged 12". This time with the final e. Pietro cut out a copy and stuck it on the trattoria fridge, next to the menu of the day.

That evening Bellini opened his black notebook and wrote under the date: "Today Pietro explained to me the difference between news and a rumour. News has two sources. A rumour has a hundred, and none of them is true. Then he told me the trattoria is news, not a rumour: it has been there for seventy-two years, and everyone who has eaten there confirms it. I didn't know what to answer. I just wrote, and I decided that I will speak at the meeting too."
